title: حِكَايَةُ الْيَهُودِيِّ
titleEn: The Steward's Tale ends; the Jew's Tale begins: the Young Man with the Severed Hand
part: Night 28 · The Steward's Tale ends / The Jew's Tale begins
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 223–232 (Night 28, continuing directly from nights-27), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 28 resumes in the middle of the steward's tale: the young man who smuggled himself into the caliph's palace in a chest recites the confession of faith, Lady Zubayda takes him in, and he is married to the lady. At the wedding feast he eats the zīr-bāja without washing his hands, and his bride, in a fury, has him beaten and, ten days later, cuts off his thumbs; he vows to wash forty times with three kinds of cleanser before touching it again. The King of China is unmoved: the hunchback's story is better, and all will hang. The Jewish physician then steps forward with a tale of his own: a young man in Damascus whose right hand has been cut off tells how, a Mosul merchant's son in Cairo and Damascus, he took up with two women, one of whom killed the other out of jealousy. The night ends mid-tale as the broker returns with word that the necklace he sold is made of brass. Verse is copied as printed. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some of the Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الثَّامِنَةُ وَالْعِشْرُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-thāminatu wa-al-ʿishrūna
sentences.l: So when it was the night, the eighth and the twenty
sentences.i: And when it was the twenty-eighth night,
sentences.n: The night formula. The tens take nominative -ūna as printed, though the ordinal agrees with a feminine 'night'.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُ أَنَّ الشَّابَّ لَمَّا قَالَ أَشْهَدُ أَنْ لَا إِلَهَ إِلَّا اللَّهُ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna al-shābba lammā qāla ashhadu an lā ilāha illā al-llāhu
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the fortunate, that the youth, when he said, 'I bear-witness that there-is-no god but God,'
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that when the young man said, 'I bear witness that there is no god but God,'
sentences.n: Shahrazād resumes. The sentence is cut here at the edge of the section; its main verb follows in the next unit, which opens with a fresh qāla.

sentences.t: قَالَ وَسَمِعْتُ الْجَارِيَةَ تَقُولُ هَذِهِ الصَّنَادِيقُ فِيهَا وَدَاعَةٌ وَشَيٌّ مِنَ الثِّيَابِ لِلسِّتِّ زُبَيْدَةَ وَتُرِيدَانِ لَا يَطَّلِعُ عَلَيْهَا أَحَدٌ
sentences.tr: qāla wa-samiʿtu al-jāriyata taqūlu hādhihi al-ṣanādīqu fīhā wadāʿatun wa-shayyun mina al-thiyābi li-al-sitti Zubaydata wa-turīdāni lā yaṭṭaliʿu ʿalayhā aḥadun
sentences.l: He said: and I heard the girl saying, 'These chests, in them is wadāʿa and a thing of the garments for the lady Zubayda, and you-two want, no one looks upon them.'
sentences.i: He said: And I heard the girl say, 'These chests hold gifts and some garments for Lady Zubayda, and you wish that no one look upon them.'
sentences.n: Three things to notice. shayy is the printed شي (for shayʾ, 'thing') pointed as the text spells it. wadāʿa as printed means 'gentleness, ease'; the sense wants wadīʿa, 'a deposit, a thing in trust' (compare wadīʿat Allāh a few lines on), so the word may be a slip, but I keep it as printed. And wa-turīdāni is a dual 'you two want', which does not fit the speaker's address; the form is obscure or corrupt (perhaps for wa-turīdu 'and she wants'), and la yaṭṭaliʿu has the indicative where Classical would have the subjunctive.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْخَلِيفَةُ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ فَتْحِهِمْ وَأَنْظُرُ مَا فِيهِمْ ثُمَّ صَرَخَ عَلَى الْخُدَّامِ وَقَالَ قَدِّمُوا الصَّنَادِيقَ عِنْدِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-khalīfatu lā budda min fatḥihim wa-anẓuru mā fīhim thumma ṣarakha ʿalā al-khuddāmi wa-qāla qaddimū al-ṣanādīqa ʿindī
sentences.l: Then the caliph said, 'There-is-no-escape from their opening, and I look at what is in them.' Then he cried out upon the servants and said, 'Bring-forward the chests to me.'
sentences.i: Then the caliph said, 'They must be opened, and I shall see what is in them.' And he shouted to the servants, 'Bring the chests before me!'
sentences.n: wa-anẓuru is printed without a vowel-letter and could be read as an imperative or as a subjunctive; I read it as an indicative continuing the thought (Middle Arabic coordination), 'and I look'.

sentences.t: فَأَيْقَنْتُ بِالْهَلَاكِ وَلَامَحَالَةَ وَغِبْتُ عَنِ الدُّنْيَا
sentences.tr: fa-ayqantu bi-al-halāki wa-lāmaḥālata wa-ghibtu ʿani al-dunyā
sentences.l: So I became-certain of the destruction, and no-doubt, and I was-absent from the world.
sentences.i: Then I was certain of my destruction, beyond all doubt, and I passed out of the world.
sentences.n: ayqana bi- 'be certain of' takes bi-. wa-lāmaḥāla, 'and without fail', is printed as one word. 'Absent from the world' means he fainted.

sentences.t: فَجَعَلَتِ الْخُدَّامُ يُقَدِّمُونَ وَاحِدًا بَعْدَ وَاحِدٍ وَهُوَ يَرَى فِيهِمُ الْعِطْرَ وَالْقُمَاشَ وَالثِّيَابَ الْفَاخِرَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-jaʿalati al-khuddāmu yuqaddimūna wāḥidan baʿda wāḥidin wa-huwa yarā fīhimu al-ʿiṭra wa-al-qumāsha wa-al-thiyāba al-fākhirata
sentences.l: So the servants began bringing-forward one after one, and he sees in them the perfume and the cloth and the splendid garments,
sentences.i: So the servants began to bring them forward one after another, and he saw in them perfumes and fine cloth and splendid garments,
sentences.n: jaʿalati is feminine singular before a plural subject, which Classical allows; the verb is then followed by yuqaddimūna with a plural. The tense slips from past to present ('he sees') as often in this narrative.

sentences.t: وَلَا زَالُوا يَفْتَحُونَ الصَّنَادِيقَ وَهُوَ يَرَى مَا فِيهِمْ مِنَ الْأَثْوَابِ وَغَيْرِهَا حَتَّى لَمْ يَبْقَ إِلَّا الصُّنْدُوقُ الَّذِي أَنَا فِيهِ وَمَدُّوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ لِيَفْتَحُوهُ
sentences.tr: wa-lā zālū yaftaḥūna al-ṣanādīqa wa-huwa yarā mā fīhim mina al-athwābi wa-ghayrihā ḥattā lam yabqa illā al-ṣundūqu alladhī anā fīhi wa-maddū aydiyahum li-yaftaḥūhu
sentences.l: And they did not cease opening the chests while he sees what is in them of the garments and other-than-them, until there did not remain but the chest which I was in, and they stretched their hands to open it.
sentences.i: And they went on opening the chests while he looked at the garments and other things inside them, until nothing remained but the chest I was in, and they stretched out their hands to open it.
sentences.n: lā zālū for Classical mā zālū, 'they did not cease', is a Middle Arabic habit.

sentences.t: فَأَسْرَعَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ وَأَتَتْ لِلْخَلِينَةِ وَقَالَتْ هَذَا الَّذِي تَرَاهُ قُدَّامَكَ فَهُوَ قُدَّامَ السِّتِّ زُبَيْدَهْ وَهُوَ الَّذِي فِيهِ سِرُّهَا
sentences.tr: fa-asraʿati al-jāriyatu wa-atat li-al-khalīnati wa-qālat hādhā alladhī tarāhu quddāmaka fa-huwa quddāma al-sitti Zubaydah wa-huwa alladhī fīhi sirruhā
sentences.l: So the girl hurried and came to the khalīna and said, 'This which you see before you, it is before the lady Zubayda, and it is that in which is her secret.'
sentences.i: Then the girl hurried and came to the caliph and said, 'This one you see before you stands before Lady Zubayda, and it is the one that holds her secret.'
sentences.n: al-khalīna is printed so; it is plainly a compositor's slip for al-khalīfa, 'the caliph' (the context leaves no doubt), and I keep the printed letters. Zubayda is spelled with final hāʾ here.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ كَلَامَهَا أَمَرَ بِإِدْخَالِ الصَّنَادِيقِ فَأَتَوُا الْخُدَّامُ وَحَمَلُونِي بِالصُّنْدُوقِ الَّذِي أَنَا فِيهِ وَوَضَعُونِي فِي وَسْطِ الْقَاعَةِ بَيْنَ الصَّنَادِيقِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa kalāmahā amara bi-idkhāli al-ṣanādīqi fa-atawu al-khuddāmu wa-ḥamalūnī bi-al-ṣundūqi alladhī anā fīhi wa-waḍaʿūnī fī wasaṭi al-qāʿati bayna al-ṣanādīqi
sentences.l: So when he heard her speech, he commanded the bringing-in of the chests, and they came, the servants, and carried me with the chest which I was in, and set me in the middle of the hall among the chests.
sentences.i: When he heard her words he ordered the chests carried in, and the servants came and bore me up, chest and all, and set me down in the middle of the hall among the chests.
sentences.n: fa-atawu al-khuddāmu and wa-ḥamalūnī put a plural verb before its subject, and the verb takes the plural ending even so (the 'akalūnī al-barāghīth' construction): a feature of Middle Arabic. amara bi- 'command' takes bi- here.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ نَشِفَ رِيقِى
sentences.tr: wa-kāna nashifa rīqī
sentences.l: And my spittle had dried.
sentences.i: My mouth had gone dry.
sentences.n: Printed with final yāʾ without dots (ى); I keep it. The verb nashifa, 'be dry', is read as a pluperfect after kāna.

sentences.t: فَأَخْرَجَتْنِي صَاحِبَتِي وَقَالَتْ مَا عَلَيْكَ بَأْسٌ وَلَاخَوْفٌ فَاشْرَحْ صَدْرَكَ وَطَيِّبْ قَلْبَكَ وَاجْلِسْ حَتَّى تَأْتِيَ السِّتُّ زُبَيْدَةُ لَعَلَّ أَنْ يَكُونَ لَكَ نَصِيبٌ فِي
sentences.tr: fa-akhrajatnī ṣāḥibatī wa-qālat mā ʿalayka baʾsun wa-lākhawfun fa-ishraḥ ṣadraka wa-ṭayyib qalbaka wa-ijlis ḥattā taʾtiya al-sittu Zubaydatu laʿalla an yakūna laka naṣībun fī
sentences.l: So my companion brought me out and said, 'There is no harm upon you and no fear, so open your chest and make-good your heart and sit until the lady Zubayda comes; perhaps there will be for you a share in',
sentences.i: Then my beloved brought me out and said, 'You have nothing to fear, no harm and no dread. Ease your breast and gladden your heart, and sit until Lady Zubayda comes; perhaps there will be a share for you in',
sentences.n: The unit ends on a dangling fī with nothing after it; a word has evidently dropped out of the print, and I do not guess it. sharaḥa ṣadrahu, 'open one's breast', is the idiom for putting oneself at ease. laʿalla an with a following verb is a Middle Arabic extension of laʿalla.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسْتُ سَاعَةً وَإِذَا بِعَشَرَةِ جَوَارٍ أَبْكَارٍ كَأَنَّهُنَّ الْأَ قْمَارُ قَدْأَ قْبَلْنَ وَاصْطَفَيْنَ خَمْسَةً مُقَابِلِينَ لِخَمْسَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-jalastu sāʿatan wa-idhā bi-ʿasharati jawārin abkārin ka-annahunna al-aqmāru qad aqbalna wa-iṣṭafayna khamsatan muqābilīna li-khamsatin
sentences.l: So I sat an hour, and behold, with ten girls, virgins, as-though-they the moons, had come-forward and ranged-themselves, five facing five.
sentences.i: So I sat for an hour, and behold, ten maidens, virgins, like moons, had come in and drawn up in two ranks, five facing five.
sentences.n: Two words are broken in the print: 'al-aqmār' appears as al-ā qmār and 'qad aqbalna' as qadā qbalna. I vocalise the letters as printed, giving the stray alif its hamza and leaving the rest of each word bare of an initial vowel. wa-idhā bi-, 'and behold, [there were]', marks the sudden appearance; the bi- is not governed by anything. ʿashara jawārin: the noun after 'ten' should be in the genitive plural; Classical would more often use the singular, but the printed plural is found.

sentences.t: وَإِذَا بِعِشْرِينَ جَارِيَةً أُخْرَى وَهُنَّ نُهَّدٌ أَبْكَارٌ وَبَيْنَهُمُ السِّتُّ زُبَيْدَةُ وَهِىَ لَمْ تَقْدِرْ تَمْشِي مِمَّا عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الْحُلِيِّ وَالْحُلَلِ
sentences.tr: wa-idhā bi-ʿishrīna jāriyatan ukhrā wa-hunna nuhhadun abkārun wa-baynahumu al-sittu Zubaydatu wa-hiya lam taqdir tamshī mimmā ʿalayhā mina al-ḥuliyyi wa-al-ḥulali
sentences.l: And behold, with twenty girls other, and they high-breasted virgins, and between them the lady Zubayda, and she was-not able, she-walks, from-that which was on her of the jewels and the robes.
sentences.i: And behold, twenty other girls, full-breasted virgins, and in their midst Lady Zubayda, who could hardly walk for the weight of the jewels and robes she wore.
sentences.n: nuhhad (plural of nāhid) are girls whose breasts are firm and risen; the word is frank, and I translate it as it stands. lam taqdir tamshī is two imperfects side by side with no linking particle, a common Middle Arabic way to say 'she could not walk'.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَقْبَلَتْ تَفَرَّقَتِ الْجَوَارِ مِنْ حَوَا لَيْهَا فَأَتَيْتُ أَنَا إِلَيْهَا وَقَبَّلْتُ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا فَأَشَارَتْ لِي بِالْجُلُوسِ فَجَلَسْتُ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā aqbalat tafarraqati al-jawāri min ḥawā layhā fa-ataytu anā ilayhā wa-qabbaltu al-arḍa bayna yadayhā fa-ashārat lī bi-al-julūsi fa-jalastu bayna yadayhā
sentences.l: So when she approached, the girls scattered from around her, and I came, I, to her, and kissed the ground between her hands, and she signalled to me with the sitting, and I sat between her hands.
sentences.i: When she drew near the girls parted from around her, and I went to her and kissed the ground before her, and she signalled to me to sit, and I sat before her.
sentences.n: 'Between her hands' is the Arabic idiom for 'in her presence'. al-jawāri is printed without its final yāʾ, as in the dialect; ḥawā layhā is a break in the print for ḥawālayhā, 'around her' (the dual of ḥawl).

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَرَعَتْ تَسْأَلُنِى وَتَسْأَلُ عَنْ نَسَبِي فَأَجَبْتُهَا عَمَّا سَأَلَتْنِي عَنْهُ فَفَرِحَتْ وَقَالَتْ مَا خَابَتْ تَرْبِيَتُنَا فِيكِ أَيُّهَا الْجَارِيَةُ
sentences.tr: thumma sharaʿat tasʾalunī wa-tasʾalu ʿan nasabī fa-ajabtuhā ʿammā saʾaltanī ʿanhu fa-fariḥat wa-qālat mā khābat tarbiyatunā fīki ayyuhā al-jāriyatu
sentences.l: Then she began to ask me and to ask about my lineage, and I answered her about what she asked me concerning, and she rejoiced and said, 'Our upbringing has not failed in you, O girl.'
sentences.i: Then she began to question me about my descent, and I answered all she asked, and she was glad and said, 'Our care has not been wasted on you, O girl.'
sentences.n: ayyuhā al-jāriya is printed with the masculine ayyuhā; and the kāf of fīki could be either gender. I read it as addressed to the girl, since the 'upbringing' was hers; but the text could also mean the young man, and I cannot tell. tasʾalunī here has the final yāʾ printed as ى.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَتْ اعْلَمْ أَنَّ هَذِهِ الْجَارِيَةَ عِنْدَنَا بِمَنْزِلَةِ الْوَلَدِ وَهِيَ وَدِيعَةُ اللَّهِ عِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: thumma qālat iʿlam anna hādhihi al-jāriyata ʿindanā bi-manzilati al-waladi wa-hiya wadīʿatu al-llāhi ʿindaka
sentences.l: Then she said: Know that this girl is with us in the rank of the child, and she is God's trust with you.
sentences.i: Then she said, 'Know that this girl is to us as a child, and she is God's trust in your keeping.'

sentences.t: فَقَبَّلْتُ الْأَرْضَ قُدَّامَهَا وَرَضِيتُ بِزَوَاجِي ثُمَّ أَمَرَتْنِى أَنْ أُقِيمَ عِنْدَهُمْ عَشَرَةَ أَيَّامٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qabbaltu al-arḍa quddāmahā wa-raḍītu bi-zawājī thumma amaratnī an uqīma ʿindahum ʿasharata ayyāmin
sentences.l: So I kissed the ground before her, and I was-content with my marriage, then she commanded me that I stay with them ten days.
sentences.i: So I kissed the ground before her and gladly accepted the marriage, and then she bade me stay with them for ten days.

sentences.t: فَأَقَمْتُ عِنْدَهُمْ هَذِهِ الْمُدَّةَ وَأَنَا لَارَى الْجَارِيَةَ إِلَّا أَنَّ بَعْضَ الْوَصَائِفِ تَأْتِينِى بِالْغَدَاءِ وَالْعَشَاءِ
sentences.tr: fa-aqamtu ʿindahum hādhihi al-muddata wa-anā lārā al-jāriyata illā anna baʿḍa al-waṣāʾifi taʾtīnī bi-al-ghadāʾi wa-al-ʿashāʾi
sentences.l: So I stayed with them this term, and I, no-I-see the girl, except that some of the maidservants came to me with the lunch and the supper.
sentences.i: So I stayed with them all that time, and I never saw the girl, save that some of the maidservants would bring me my midday meal and my supper.
sentences.n: lārā is lā arā, 'I do not see', written as one word. ghadāʾ and ʿashāʾ are the morning and evening meals. taʾtīnī bi- 'bring' takes bi-, since ātā bi- means 'come with, bring'.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ هَذِهِ الْمُدَّةِ شَاوَرَتِ السِّتُّ زُبَيْدَةُ الْخَلِيفَةَ فِي زَوَاجِ جَارِيَتِهَا فَأَذِنَ لَهَا وَأَمَرَ لَهَا بِعَشَرَةِ آلَافِ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda hādhihi al-muddati shāwarati al-sittu Zubaydatu al-khalīfata fī zawāji jāriyatihā fa-adhina lahā wa-amara lahā bi-ʿasharati ālāfi dīnārin
sentences.l: And after this term the lady Zubayda consulted the caliph about the marriage of her girl, and he permitted her and commanded for her ten thousand dinars.
sentences.i: After this time Lady Zubayda consulted the caliph about the marriage of her maid, and he gave her leave and ordered for her ten thousand dinars.
sentences.n: amara lahā bi- means 'ordered [a payment] for her' (the money named with bi-). Note that ten takes the genitive of the plural 'thousands', then 'dinar'.

sentences.t: فَأَرْسَلَتِ السِّتُّ زُبَيْدَةُ خَلْفَ الشُّهُودِ وَالْقَاضِي وَكَتَبُوا كِتَابِي عَلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: fa-arsalati al-sittu Zubaydatu khalfa al-shuhūdi wa-al-qāḍī wa-katabū kitābī ʿalayhā
sentences.l: So the lady Zubayda sent after the witnesses and the judge, and they wrote my writing upon her.
sentences.i: So Lady Zubayda sent for the witnesses and the judge, and they drew up my marriage contract with her.
sentences.n: kataba kitābahu ʿalā means 'to write the marriage contract to [a woman]'. Here the witnesses are the legal witnesses (shuhūd), the same word that gave 'al-shāhid' earlier in the frame.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ عَمِلُوا الْحَلْوِيَّاتِ وَالْأَ طْعِمَةَ الْفَاخِرَةَ وَفَرَّقُوا عَلَى سَائِرِ الْبُيُوتِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika ʿamilū al-ḥalwiyyāti wa-al-aṭʿimata al-fākhirata wa-farraqū ʿalā sāʾiri al-buyūti
sentences.l: And after that they made the sweets and the splendid foods and distributed them upon the rest of the houses.
sentences.i: After that they prepared sweetmeats and splendid dishes, and sent them round to all the other houses.
sentences.n: al-aṭʿima is broken in the print (al-ā ṭʿima).

sentences.t: وَمَكَثُوا عَلَى هَذَا الْحَالِ عَشَرَةَ أَيَّامٍ أُخَرَ وَبَعْدَ الْعِشْرِينَ يَوْمًا دَخَلَتِ الْجَارِيَةُ الْحَمَّامَ
sentences.tr: wa-makathū ʿalā hādhā al-ḥāli ʿasharata ayyāmin ukhara wa-baʿda al-ʿishrīna yawman dakhalati al-jāriyatu al-ḥammāma
sentences.l: And they remained upon this state ten days other, and after the twenty days the girl entered the bath.
sentences.i: And they went on in this way for ten more days, and after the twenty days the bride went into the bath.
sentences.n: ḥāl is made masculine (hādhā) as is usual. 'The girl' is now the bride.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ قَدَّمُوا خُونْجَهْ فِيهَا طَعَامٌ وَمِنْ جُمْلَتِهِ خَافِقِيَّةٌ زِيرْبَاجَةٌ مَحْشِيَّةٌ بِالسُّكَّرِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum qaddamū khūnjah fīhā ṭaʿāmun wa-min jumlatihi khāfiqiyyatun zīrbājatun maḥshiyyatun bi-al-sukkari
sentences.l: Then they brought-forward a khūnja in which was food, and among its sum a khāfiqiyya, a zīrbāja stuffed with the sugar,
sentences.i: Then they brought in a tray with food on it, and among the dishes a khāfiqiyya, a zīrbāja stuffed with sugar,
sentences.n: khūnja is a tray (Persian khwānča) and the zīrbāja is the sweet-and-sour meat dish that gave Night 27 its start. khāfiqiyya I cannot identify with confidence; it may be a kind of dish or a cover for one, and I leave it untranslated. mina jumlatihi 'among it' is 'of its total'. The text has bi-al-sukkar for the stuffing.

sentences.t: وَعَلَيْهَا الْمَاوَرْدُ الْمُمَسَّكُ وَفِيهَا صُدُورُ الدَّجَاجِ الْمُحَمَّرَةِ وَبَقِيَّةُ الْأَلْوَانِ مِمَّايُدْهِشُ الْعُقُولَ
sentences.tr: wa-ʿalayhā al-māwardu al-mumassaku wa-fīhā ṣudūru al-dajāji al-muḥammarati wa-baqiyyatu al-alwāni mimmāyudhishu al-ʿuqūla
sentences.l: And on it the rose-water the musked, and in it the breasts of the fowl the browned, and the remainder of the kinds, of-that-which dazzles the minds.
sentences.i: Over it was musk-scented rosewater, and in it breasts of roasted fowl, and the rest of the dishes, such as dazzle the mind.
sentences.n: al-muḥammara agrees with the feminine singular rather than the plural dajāj, a collective. mimmāyudhishu is printed as one word, 'of that which astounds'.

sentences.t: فَوَاللَّهِ مَا أَمْهَلْتُ دُونَ أَنْ بَرَكْتُ عَلَى الزِّيرْبَاجَةِ وَأَكَلْتُ مِنْهَا بِحَسَبِ الْكِفَايَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-wa-allāhi mā amhaltu dūna an baraktu ʿalā al-zīrbājati wa-akaltu minhā bi-ḥasabi al-kifāyati
sentences.l: And by God, I did not delay, short of that I knelt upon the zīrbāja and ate of it according to sufficiency.
sentences.i: By God, I did not wait a moment before I fell upon the zīrbāja and ate of it as much as I needed.
sentences.n: mā amhaltu dūna an, 'I did not delay before', is the idiom. barakta ʿalā 'knelt upon', the camel's kneeling, is the word for settling to a dish. The sentence runs on into the next unit.

sentences.t: وَمَسَحْتُ يَدَيَّ وَنَسِيتُ أَنْ أَغْسِلَهُمَا وَتَمَيْتُ جَالِسًا إِلَى أَنْ دَخَلَ الظَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: wa-masaḥtu yadayya wa-nasītu an aghsilahumā wa-tamaytu jālisan ilā an dakhala al-ẓalāmu
sentences.l: and I-wiped my-two-hands and I-forgot that I-wash them-two, and I-remained sitting until entered the darkness
sentences.i: I wiped my hands and forgot to wash them, and I sat on until darkness fell.
sentences.n: tamaytu is a Middle Arabic form of 'I remained' (Classical tammaytu or tamamtu), here followed by a circumstantial accusative: 'I remained sitting'. The young man is at the wedding feast, having just eaten the zīrbāja (a sweet-sour dish) without washing his hands.

sentences.t: وَأُوقِدَتِ الشُّمُوعُ وَأَقْبَلَتِ الْمَغَانِي بِالدُّفُوفِ وَلَمْ يَزَالُوا يَجْلُونَ الْعَرُوسَةَ وَيُنَقِّطُونَ بِالذَّهَبِ حَتَّى طَافَتِ الْقَصْرَ كُلَّهُ
sentences.tr: wa-ūqidati al-shumūʿu wa-aqbalati al-maghānī bi-al-dufūfi wa-lam yazālū yajlūna al-ʿarūsata wa-yunaqqiṭūna bi-al-dhahabi ḥattā ṭāfati al-qaṣra kullahu
sentences.l: and were-kindled the candles, and approached the singing-women with the tambourines, and they-did-not cease displaying the bride and showering-with-coins with the gold, until she-circled the palace all-of-it
sentences.i: Candles were lit and the singing-women came forward with their tambourines; they did not cease to parade the bride, scattering gold coins over her, until she had gone round the whole palace.
sentences.n: al-maghānī is the plural of mughanniya, a singing-woman. The bride was paraded (tujlā) before the guests, and coins were showered on her: yunaqqiṭūna is from nuqṭ, the gift-money scattered at weddings. The subject of ṭāfat is the bride, so the verb is feminine.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ أَقْبَلُوا بِهَا وَخَفَّفُوا مَا عَلَيْهَا مِنَ الْمَلْبُوسِ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda dhālika aqbalū bihā wa-khaffafū mā ʿalayhā mina al-malbūsi
sentences.l: and after that they-approached with her and lightened what upon her of the clothing
sentences.i: After that they brought her in and lightened her of the clothing she wore.
sentences.n: aqbalū bi- is 'they brought (her) forward'; here the bi- is demanded by the verb, not a free preposition. khaffafū mā ʿalayhā: they removed some of the heavy bridal finery.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا خَلَوْتُ مَعَهَا فِي الْفِرَاشِ وَعَانَقْتُهَا وَأَنَا لَمْ أُصَدِّقْ بِوِصَالِهَا ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا شَمَّتْ فِي يَدَيَّ رَائِحَةَ الزِّيرْبَاجَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā khalawtu maʿahā fī al-firāshi wa-ʿānaqtuhā wa-anā lam uṣaddiq bi-wiṣālihā thumma innahā shammat fī yadayya rāʾiḥata al-zīrbājati
sentences.l: so when I-was-alone with her in the bedding and I-embraced her, and I, I-had-not believed in her union, then that-she smelled in my-two-hands the smell of the zīrbāja
sentences.i: When I was alone with her in bed and had embraced her, hardly believing that I had won her, she smelled the scent of the zīrbāja on my hands.
sentences.n: wa-anā lam uṣaddiq is a circumstantial clause: 'while I could not believe'. ṣaddaqa bi- 'believe in, credit' takes bi- here because the verb chooses it. Both rāʾiḥa and the later al-rāʾiḥa are printed with the precomposed hamza-on-yā, so they are kept as printed. The zīrbāja was a sauce of meat with vinegar and sugar; the smell of it on unwashed hands is what sets off the lady's rage.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا شَمَّتِ الرَّائِحَةَ صَرَخَتْ صَرْخَةً عَظِيمَةً
sentences.tr: fa-lammā shammati al-rāʾiḥata ṣarakhat ṣarkhatan ʿaẓīmatan
sentences.l: so when she-smelled the smell she-cried-out a cry great
sentences.i: When she smelled it, she gave a great cry.

sentences.t: فَنَزَلَتْ لَهَا الْجَوَارِ مِنْ كُلِّ جَانِبٍ فَارْتَجَفْتُ وَلَمْ أَعْلَمْ مَا الْخَبَرُ
sentences.tr: fa-nazalat lahā al-jawāri min kulli jānibin fa-irtajaftu wa-lam aʿlam mā al-khabaru
sentences.l: so descended to her the girls from every side, so I-trembled, and I-did-not know what the news
sentences.i: At that the slave-girls came running to her from every side, and I trembled, not knowing what the matter was.
sentences.n: al-jawār is printed without the final yā' of al-jawārī (slave-girls, plural of jāriya); the vocalisation carries the kasra the missing letter would have borne, and the form recurs below. nazalat lahā 'came down to her' is an idiom for rushing to someone's help.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتِ الْجَوَارِ مَالَكِ يَا أُخْتَنَا فَقَالَتْ لَهُنَّ أَخْرِجُوا هَذَا الْمَجْنُونَ عَنِّي فَأَنَا أَحْسِبُ أَنَّهُ عَاقِلٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qālati al-jawāri mā laki yā ukhtanā fa-qālat lahunna akhrijū hādhā al-majnūna ʿannī fa-anā aḥsibu annahu ʿāqilun
sentences.l: so said the girls: What to-you, O our-sister? So she-said to-them: Remove this madman from me, for I, I reckon that-he sane
sentences.i: The girls said, “What ails you, our sister?” And she said to them, “Take this madman away from me! I had thought him sane.”
sentences.n: mā laki, literally 'what (is) to you', is the ordinary 'what is the matter with you?'. aḥsibu is present tense, 'I reckon', but the sense is of a mistake just discovered, so the English puts it in the past.

sentences.t: قُلْتُ لَهَا وَمَا الَّذِي ظَهَرَ لَكِ مِنْ جُنُونِي
sentences.tr: qultu lahā wa-mā alladhī ẓahara laki min junūnī
sentences.l: I-said to-her: And what that-which appeared to-you of my-madness?
sentences.i: I said to her, “And what sign of madness have you seen in me?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ يَا مَجْنُونُ لَايْشْ أَكَلْتَ مِنَ الزِّيرْبَاجَةِ وَلَمْ تَغْسِلْ يَدَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālat yā majnūn lāysh akalta mina al-zīrbājati wa-lam taghsil yadaka
sentences.l: so she-said: O madman, why did-you-eat of the zīrbāja and you-did-not wash your-hand?
sentences.i: She said, “You madman! Why did you eat of the zīrbāja without washing your hand?”
sentences.n: lāysh is the colloquial 'why?', a contraction of li-ayyi shayʾin ('for what thing'), the same word as Levantine lēsh. It is spoken-register Arabic in a literary frame, a Middle Arabic feature. akala min means 'ate of, ate some of'.

sentences.t: فَوَاللَّهِ لَأُجَازِيكَ عَلَى فِعْلِكَ أَمِثْلُكَ يَدْخُلُ عَلَى مِثْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-wa-allāhi la-ujāzīka ʿalā fiʿlika a-mithluka yadkhulu ʿalā mithlī
sentences.l: so by-God I-will-requite-you for your-deed: Is-one-like-you to-enter upon one-like-me?
sentences.i: By God, I will repay you for what you have done! Does one such as you come in to one such as me?
sentences.n: The la- on the verb is the oath's answer ('I will surely repay you'). The printed verb has no nūn of emphasis, so it is vocalised as a plain indicative. dakhala ʿalā 'enter upon' is the idiom for a husband going in to his bride, so mithlī is 'a woman of my rank'.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ تَنَاوَلَتْ مِنْ جَانِبِهَا سَوْطًا مَضْفُورًا وَنَزَلَتْ بِهِ عَلَى ظَهْرِي ثُمَّ عَلَى مَقَاعِدِي حَتَّى غِبْتُ أَنَا مِنَ الدُّنْيَا مِنْ كَثْرَةِ الضَّرْبِ
sentences.tr: thumma tanāwalat min jānibihā sawṭan maḍfūran wa-nazalat bihi ʿalā ẓahrī thumma ʿalā maqāʿidī ḥattā ghibtu anā mina al-dunyā min kathrati al-ḍarbi
sentences.l: then she-took from her-side a-whip plaited, and she-came-down with-it on my-back, then on my-seat-parts, until I-was-absent, I, from the world from the-abundance of-the beating
sentences.i: Then she took from beside her a plaited whip and brought it down on my back, and then on my backside, until, from the sheer quantity of blows, I lost all sense of the world.
sentences.n: maqāʿid, 'seats', is the frank word for the buttocks, and is rendered frankly. nazalat bi- 'brought (it) down with'; here bi- marks the instrument carried down onto the victim. ghibtu min al-dunyā 'I was absent from the world' means that he passed out.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهَا قَالَتْ لِلْجَوَارِ خُذُوهُ وَامْضُوا بِهِ إِلَى مُتَوَلِّى الْمَدِينَةِ يَقْطَعُ يَدَهُ الَّتِي أَكَلَ بِهَا الزِّيرْبَاجَةَ وَلَمْ يَغْسِلْهَا
sentences.tr: thumma innahā qālat li-al-jawāri khudhūhu wa-imḍū bihi ilā mutawallī al-madīnati yaqṭaʿu yadahu allatī akala bihā al-zīrbājata wa-lam yaghsilhā
sentences.l: then that-she said to-the girls: Take-him and go with-him to the governor of the city, that-he-cut his-hand which he-ate with-it the zīrbāja and he-did-not wash-it
sentences.i: Then she said to the girls, “Take him and go with him to the governor of the city, that he may cut off the hand with which he ate the zīrbāja and did not wash.”
sentences.n: mutawallī al-madīna is the city's governor, here the official who carries out punishments. The printed ending is ى, so the word keeps it; the kasra of the vocalisation shows the sound -ī. yaqṭaʿu is a bare indicative where Classical would use a purpose clause (li-yaqṭaʿa or a subjunctive): a Middle Arabic feature. amḍū bihi, 'go off with him', takes bi- because the verb does.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ ذَلِكَ قُلْتُ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ تُقْطَعُ يَدِي مِنْ أَجْلِ أَكْلِ الزِّيرْبَاجَةِ وَلَاغَسَلْتُهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu dhālika qultu lāḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-allāhi tuqṭaʿu yadī min ajli akli al-zīrbājati wa-lāghasaltuhā
sentences.l: so when I-heard that I-said: There-is-no-might and no power except with God! Is-cut my-hand on account of eating the zīrbāja and not-I-washed-it?
sentences.i: When I heard that, I said, “There is no might and no power but in God! Is my hand to be cut off for eating the zīrbāja and not washing it?”
sentences.n: The phrase lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-llāh is the standard cry of dismay; its first lā is printed attached to ḥawla. The last word, wa-lāghasaltuhā, is printed as one word: wa-lā + the perfect 'I washed it', 'and (I) did not wash it', continuing the reason clause. I take it that way; the sense is certain, the grammar slightly compressed. tuqṭaʿu has no question particle: the question is carried by tone.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلْنَ عَلَيْهَا الْجَوَارِ وَقُلْنَ لَهَا يَا أُخْتَنَا لَا تُؤَاخِذِيهِ بِفِعْلِهِ هَذِهِ الْمَرَّةَ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalna ʿalayhā al-jawāri wa-qulna lahā yā ukhtanā lā tuʾākhidhīhi bi-fiʿlihi hādhihi al-marrata
sentences.l: so entered-they upon her the girls, and they-said to-her: O our-sister, do-not hold-him-to-account for his-deed this time
sentences.i: Then the girls came in to her and said, “Our sister, do not hold him to account for what he has done, this once.”
sentences.n: The verb comes first and carries the feminine plural ending (dakhalna), then the subject al-jawār follows: the agreeing verb before its plural subject is a Middle Arabic habit. ākhadha (III) bi- 'to take (someone) to task for' takes bi- of the thing charged: bi-fiʿlihi, 'for his act'. The attached -hi and bare hādhihi are as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَتْ وَاللَّهِ لَا بُدَّأَنْ أَقْطَعَ شَيْئًا مِنْ أَطْرَافِهِ ثُمَّ رَاحَتْ وَغَابَتْ عَشَرَةَ أَيَّامٍ وَلَمْ أَرَهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qālat wa-allāhi lā buddaan aqṭaʿa shayʾan min aṭrāfihi thumma rāḥat wa-ghābat ʿasharata ayyāmin wa-lam arahā
sentences.l: so she-said: By-God, no escape-that I-cut something of his-extremities! Then she-went, and was-absent ten days, and I-did-not see-her
sentences.i: She said, “By God, I must cut off some part of his extremities!” Then she went away and was gone ten days, and I did not see her.
sentences.n: lā budda an, 'it cannot be avoided that', is printed lā budda-an with the last two words run together; the vocalisation follows the print, with the alif carrying its hamza. aṭrāf, 'extremities', is a euphemism of her own speech: she means fingers, hands, or worse, and is true to her word below.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ الْعَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ أَقْبَلَتْ عَلَيَّ وَقَالَتْ لِي يَا أَسْوَدَ الْوَجْهِ أَنَا أُصْلِحُ لَكَ كَيْفَ تَأْكُلُ الزِّيرْبَاجَةَ وَلَمْ تَغْسِلْ يَدَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda al-ʿasharati ayyāmin aqbalat ʿalayya wa-qālat lī yā aswada al-wajhi anā uṣliḥu laka kayfa taʾkulu al-zīrbājata wa-lam taghsil yadaka
sentences.l: and after the ten days she-approached upon me and said to-me: O black-of-the-face, I, I-will-set-right for-you how you-eat the zīrbāja and you-did-not wash your-hand
sentences.i: And after those ten days she came to me and said, “You blackguard! I shall teach you what it is to eat the zīrbāja without washing your hand!”
sentences.n: al-ʿashara ayyām: the numeral carries the article and is followed by the counted noun in the genitive; this is not Classical (which would have al-ayyām al-ʿashara or ʿasharat ayyām) but is as printed. yā aswada al-wajhi, 'black of face', is a standard insult meaning 'shameless one, disgraced one'. uṣliḥu laka is colloquial: 'I'll fix you, I'll sort you out'. kayfa here introduces the offence, not a real question.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ صَرَخَتْ عَلَى الْجَوَارِ فَكَتَّفُونِي وَأَخَذَتْ مُوسَى مَا ضِيًا وَقَطَعَتْ إِبْهَا مَاتِي
sentences.tr: thumma ṣarakhat ʿalā al-jawāri fa-kattafūnī wa-akhadhat mūsā mā ḍiyan wa-qaṭaʿat ibhā mātī
sentences.l: then she-cried-out upon the girls, so they-bound-me, and she-took a-razor sharp, and she-cut my-thumbs
sentences.i: Then she called out to the girls, and they bound me; and she took a sharp razor and cut off my thumbs,
sentences.n: ṣarakha ʿalā means 'shouted at (to summon)'. Two words are split by a space in the print: mā ḍiyan is mā + ḍiyan for māḍiyan, 'sharp', and ibhā mātī is ibhā + mātī for ibhāmātī, 'my thumbs'. We keep the print's break and vocalise each half so that the word is recognisable when the two are read together. ibhāmāt is a plural of ibhām, 'thumb', with the pronoun -ī; Classical would use the dual.

sentences.t: كَمَا تَرَوْنَ يَا جَمَاعَةُ
sentences.tr: kamā tarawna yā jamāʿatu
sentences.l: as you-see, O company
sentences.i: as you see, my friends.
sentences.n: He holds up his hands to the guests at the feast: this is the story of the missing thumbs, told in the first person to the diners.

sentences.t: فَغُشِيَ عَلَيَّ ثُمَّ ذَرَّتْ عَلَيْهِ بِالذَّرُورِ فَانْقَطَعَ الدَّمُ
sentences.tr: fa-ghushiya ʿalayya thumma dharrat ʿalayhi bi-al-dharūri fa-inqaṭaʿa al-damu
sentences.l: so it-was-fainted upon me, then she-sprinkled upon it with-the powder, so ceased the blood
sentences.i: I fainted, and then she sprinkled the powder over the wound, and the blood stopped.
sentences.n: ghushiya ʿalayya, literally 'it was covered over upon me', is the idiom for fainting. al-dharūr is a styptic powder. dharra ʿalā X bi-Y: the bi- names what is sprinkled, so 'sprinkled the powder on it'.

sentences.t: وَجَعَلْتُ أَقُولُ مَا بَقِيتُ آكُلُ الزِّيرْبَاجَةَ حَتَّى أَغْسِلَ يَدَيَّ أَرْبَعِينَ مَرَّةً بِالْأُشْنَانِ وَأَرْبَعِينَ مَرَّةً بِالسُّعْدِ وَأَرْبَعِينَ مَرَّةً بِالصَّابُونِ
sentences.tr: wa-jaʿaltu aqūlu mā baqītu ākulu al-zīrbājata ḥattā aghsila yadayya arbaʿīna marratan bi-al-ushnāni wa-arbaʿīna marratan bi-al-suʿdi wa-arbaʿīna marratan bi-al-ṣābūni
sentences.l: and I-began I-say: I-do-not remain eating the zīrbāja until I-wash my-two-hands forty times with-the potash and forty times with-the cyperus and forty times with-the soap
sentences.i: And I began to say, “I shall never eat zīrbāja again until I have washed my hands forty times with potash, forty times with cyperus, and forty times with soap.”
sentences.n: jaʿaltu aqūlu 'I began to say' is a common aspect-verb construction. mā baqītu + imperfect, here 'as long as I live I will not eat', is idiomatic. ākulu keeps its precomposed madda as in the print. al-ushnān is potash or saltwort ash used as a detergent, al-suʿd is cyperus (nut-grass) root, used as a perfumed cleanser; the bi- of each names the washing agent.

sentences.t: فَأَخَذَتْ عَلَيَّ مِيثَاقًا أَنِّي لَا آكُلُ الزِّبْرِبَاجَةَ حَتَّى أَغْسِلَ يَدَيَّ كَمَا ذَكَرْتُ لَكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-akhadhat ʿalayya mīthāqan annī lā ākulu al-zibribājata ḥattā aghsila yadayya kamā dhakartu lakum
sentences.l: so she-took upon me a-covenant that-I do-not eat the zīrbāja until I-wash my-two-hands as I-mentioned to-you
sentences.i: And she took from me a solemn pledge that I would not eat zīrbāja until I had washed my hands as I have told you.
sentences.n: Here and in the next unit the dish is printed al-zibribāja, not al-zīrbāja as above: probably the compositor's slip, but the print is kept and vocalised as printed. akhadha ʿalā X mīthāqan is 'take an oath from X'.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا جِبْتُمْ بِهَذِةِ الزِّيرْبَاجَةِ تَغَيَّرَ لَوْنِي وَقُلْتُ فِي نَفْسِي هَذِةِ سَبَبُ قَطْعِ إِبْهَا مَاتِي
sentences.tr: fa-lammā jibtum bi-hādhihi al-zīrbājati taghayyara lawnī wa-qultu fī nafsī hādhihi sababu qaṭʿi ibhā mātī
sentences.l: so when you-brought with this zīrbāja changed my-color, and I-said in my-self: This is the cause of the cutting of my-thumbs
sentences.i: So when you brought in this zīrbāja, my color changed, and I said to myself, “This is the cause of the loss of my thumbs.”
sentences.n: jibtum is the colloquial form of Classical jiʾtum, 'you came, you brought'; jāʾa bi- 'bring' takes bi- of the thing brought, as in the idiom a-tā bi-. The edition prints hādhihi here and in the lines below as هذة with tāʾ marbūṭa; the vocalisation reads it as hādhihi, 'this' (f.). The pronoun hādhihi agrees with the feminine zīrbāja, though sabab 'cause' follows it, a lax agreement.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا غَصَبْتُمْ عَلَيَّ قُلْتُ لَابُدَّأَنْ أُوفِيَ بِمَا حَلَفْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā ghaṣabtum ʿalayya qultu lābuddaan ufiya bi-mā ḥalaftu
sentences.l: so when you-compelled upon me, I-said: no-escape-that I-fulfil what I-swore
sentences.i: But when you pressed me, I said, “I must keep what I swore.”
sentences.n: ghaṣabtum ʿalayya, 'you used force with me', here means that the company pressed him to eat. Printed lābuddaan as one word (lā budda an). awfā bi- 'to fulfil (an oath)' takes bi- of the thing fulfilled.

sentences.t: قَالَ الْحَاضِرُونَ فَمَا الَّذِي حَصَلَ لَكَ بَعْدَ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: qāla al-ḥāḍirūna fa-mā alladhī ḥaṣala laka baʿda dhālika
sentences.l: said the present-ones: So what that-which came-about to-you after that?
sentences.i: The company said, “And what befell you after that?”
sentences.n: The reply is split from the previous unit at the change of speaker; the guests of the feast interrupt the young man, who then goes on with his story.

sentences.t: قَالَ فَلَمَّا حَلَفْتُ لَهَا طَابَ قَلْبُهَا وَنِمْتُ وَإِيَّاهَا وَقَعَدْنَا مُدَّةً
sentences.tr: qāla fa-lammā ḥalaftu lahā ṭāba qalbuhā wa-nimtu wa-iyyāhā wa-qaʿadnā muddatan
sentences.l: He-said: So when I-swore to-her, was-good her-heart, and I-slept and her, and we-sat a-while
sentences.i: He said: Once I had sworn to her, her heart was eased, and I slept with her, and we stayed on for a while.
sentences.n: wa-nimtu wa-iyyāhā, 'I slept and (also) her', is the idiom for 'I slept with her', with the object pronoun iyyā- standing in for 'with'; this is frank and not a euphemism. ṭāba qalbuhā 'her heart became good' = she was appeased.

sentences.t: وَبَعْدَ الْمُدَّةِ قَالَتْ إِنَّ دَارَ الْخِلَافَةِ لَا يَحْسُنُ مَقَامُنَا فِيهَا وَمَا دَخَلَ فِيهَا غَيْرُكَ وَمَادَ خَلْتُ فِيهَا إِلَّا بِعِنَايَةِ السِّتِّ زُبَيْدَةَ
sentences.tr: wa-baʿda al-muddati qālat inna dāra al-khilāfati lā yaḥsunu maqāmunā fīhā wa-mā dakhala fīhā ghayruka wa-mād khaltu fīhā illā bi-ʿināyati al-sitti Zubaydata
sentences.l: and after the while she-said: Verily the house of the caliphate, not is-fitting our-staying in-it, and not entered in-it other-than-you, and not I-entered in-it except with the care of the Lady Zubayda
sentences.i: After a while she said, “The Caliph’s palace is no fit place for us to stay in. No one but you has ever entered it, and I myself came in only through the favor of Lady Zubayda.”
sentences.n: Two words are split by a space in the print: mād khaltu is mā dakhaltu, 'I did not enter'; the vocalisation follows the print's break as mād + khaltu. al-sitt is 'the Lady', a title of courtesy (as in Sitt Zubayda, the caliph’s wife and Hārūn’s cousin). illā bi-ʿināyati: bi- 'by means of, through'.

sentences.t: وَهِيَ أَعْطَتْنِي خَمْسِينَ أَلْفَ دِينَارٍ وَقَالَتْ لِي خُذْ هَذِةِ الدَّرَاهِمَ وَاخْرُجْ وَاشْتَرِ لَنَا دَارًا فَسِيحَةً
sentences.tr: wa-hiya aʿṭatnī khamsīna alfa dīnārin wa-qālat lī khudh hādhihi al-darāhima wa-ukhruj wa-ishtari lanā dāran fasīḥatan
sentences.l: and she, she-gave-me fifty thousand dinars and said to-me: Take this the dirhams and go-out and buy for-us a-house spacious
sentences.i: She herself gave me fifty thousand dinars, and said to me, “Take this money and go out and buy us a spacious house.”
sentences.n: The currency slips from dinars to dirhams between the two clauses, as in the print: loose use of 'money'. khamsīna alfa dīnārin: the counted noun after 'thousand' is genitive.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ وَاشْتَرَيْتُ دَارًا مَلِيحَةً فَسِيحَةً وَنَقَلْتُ جَمِيعَ مَا عِنْدَهَا فِى الدَّارِ مِنَ النِّعَمِ وَمَا ادَّخَرَتْهُ مِنَ الْأَمْوَالِ وَالْقُمَاشِ وَالتُّحَفِ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu wa-ishtaraytu dāran malīḥatan fasīḥatan wa-naqaltu jamīʿa mā ʿindahā fī al-dāri mina al-niʿami wa-mā iddakharathu mina al-amwāli wa-al-qumāshi wa-al-tuḥafi
sentences.l: so I-went-out and bought a-house handsome spacious, and I-moved all what with-her in the house of the blessings and what she-had-stored of the monies and the stuffs and the rarities
sentences.i: So I went out and bought a handsome, spacious house, and I moved into it all the comforts she had in the palace, and everything she had laid by of money, fabrics and curios.
sentences.n: The edition spells fī here with a final ى (فى), a common usage; the vocalisation reads it fī. ʿindahā fī al-dār 'what was with her in the (caliph's) house'. al-niʿam is the 'good things', comforts and furnishings. al-qumāsh is 'stuffs, cloth'; al-tuḥaf 'rarities, precious objects'. ma iddakharathu: 'what she had put by', a relative clause with the perfect.

sentences.t: فَهَذَا سَبَبُ قَطْعِ إِبْهَا مَاتِي
sentences.tr: fa-hādhā sababu qaṭʿi ibhā mātī
sentences.l: so this is the cause of the cutting of my-thumbs
sentences.i: That, then, is why my thumbs were cut off.

sentences.t: فَأَكَلْنَا وَانْصَرَفْنَا وَبَعْدَ ذَلِكَ جَرَى مَعَ الْأَحْدَبِ مَاجَرَى
sentences.tr: fa-akalnā wa-inṣarafnā wa-baʿda dhālika jarā maʿa al-aḥdabi mājarā
sentences.l: so we-ate and we-departed, and after that happened with the hunchback what happened
sentences.i: So we ate, and went our ways; and after that there came to pass with the hunchback what came to pass.
sentences.n: The young man's story ends and the steward resumes in his own voice. mājarā is printed as one word (mā jarā, 'what happened'), used as a formula for 'the whole affair, as everyone knows'. jarā maʿa X is 'befell X'.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا سَبَبُ حَدِيثِي وَالسَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā sababu ḥadīthī wa-al-salāmu
sentences.l: and this is the cause of my-talk, and the peace
sentences.i: And that is the reason for my tale; and peace.
sentences.n: wa-al-salām is the formal sign-off to a speech or letter, 'and that is all; peace'. The unit's wa-hādhā sabab is the formal closing of the steward's tale, which he started as a story for the King of China.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْمَلِكُ مَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-maliku mā
sentences.l: so said the king: What
sentences.i: Then the king said, “What
sentences.n: The king's reply breaks off here, on the negative mā; it is completed in the next unit.

sentences.t: هَذَا بِأَعْذَبَ مِنْ حَدِيثِ الْأَحْدَبِ بَلْ حَدِيثُ الْأَحْدَبِ أَعْذَبُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَلَا بُدَّ مِنْ شَنْقِكُمْ أَنْتُمُ الْجَمِيعُ
sentences.tr: hādhā bi-aʿdhaba min ḥadīthi al-aḥdabi bal ḥadīthu al-aḥdabi aʿdhabu min dhālika wa-lā budda min shanqikum antumu al-jamīʿu
sentences.l: This [is] with-sweeter than the tale of-the-hunchback; nay, the tale of-the-hunchback [is] sweeter than that, and there-is-no-escape from your hanging, you the all.
sentences.i: This is no sweeter than the hunchback's tale; nay, the hunchback's tale is sweeter than that, and hanged you shall be, every one of you.
sentences.n: The negative mā that ends the preceding unit belongs with this one: mā hādhā bi-aʿdhaba, 'this is not sweeter'. That is why the comparative carries a bi-, the bi- that follows a negated 'this is'. 'Antum al-jamīʿ' repeats the pronoun for emphasis, 'the whole lot of you'; the nominative jamīʿ after the genitive -kum is as printed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الْيَهُودِيَّ تَقَدَّمَ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ وَقَالَ يَا مَلِكَ الزَّمَانِ أَنَا أُحَدِّثُكَ بِحَدِيثٍ أَعْجَبَ مِنْ حَدِيثِ الْأَحْدَبِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-yahūdiyya taqaddama wa-qabbala al-arḍa wa-qāla yā malika al-zamāni anā uḥaddithuka bi-ḥadīthin aʿjaba min ḥadīthi al-aḥdabi
sentences.l: Then indeed the Jew came-forward and kissed the earth and said: O king of-the-age, I will-tell-you a-tale more-wondrous than the tale of-the-hunchback.
sentences.i: Then the Jew stepped forward, kissed the ground, and said: O king of the age, I shall tell you a tale more wondrous than the hunchback's.
sentences.n: Kissing the ground is the courtier's gesture before a king, and 'king of the age' is a stock address. Ḥaddatha takes its tale with bi-, so 'I tell you with a tale' simply means 'I tell you a tale'.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ مَلِكُ الصِّينِ هَاتِ مَاعِنْدَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla maliku al-Ṣīni hāti mā ʿindaka
sentences.l: Then said the king of China: Bring what [is] with-you.
sentences.i: The king of China said: Let us have what you have.
sentences.n: Hāti is the imperative 'bring', used as 'out with it'. The print joins mā ʿindaka into one word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَعْجَبُ مَاجَرَى لِي فِي شَبَابِي أَنِّي كُنْتُ فِي دِمَشْقَ الشَّامِ وَتَعَلَّمْتُ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla aʿjabu mā jarā lī fī shabābī annī kuntu fī Dimashqa al-Shāmi wa-taʿallamtu fīhā
sentences.l: So he said: The most-wondrous of-what happened to-me in my youth [is] that-I was in Damascus of-the-Levant, and I studied in-it.
sentences.i: He said: The most wondrous thing that befell me in my youth is this: I was in Damascus of Syria, and I studied there.
sentences.n: Al-Shām is Syria, the Levant, so 'Dimashq al-Shām' is simply 'Damascus of Syria'. The sentence leaves its 'is' unwritten: 'the most wondrous of what happened to me' is the subject, and 'that I was…' opens the story. The print joins mā jarā into one word.

sentences.t: فَبَيْنَمَا أَنَا جَالِسٌ فِي يَوْمٍ مِنَ الْأَيَّامِ إِذَا تَانِي مَمْلُوكٌ مِنْ بَيْتِ الصَّاحِبِ بِدِمَشْقَ وَقَالَ كَلِّمْ سَيِّدِي
sentences.tr: fa-baynamā anā jālisun fī yawmin mina al-ayyāmi idhā tānī mamlūkun min bayti al-ṣāḥibi bi-Dimashqa wa-qāla kallim sayyidī
sentences.l: So while I [was] sitting on a day of the days, behold, there-came-to-me a mamluk from the house of-the-Ṣāḥib in Damascus, and he said: Speak-with my master.
sentences.i: One day, as I was sitting, behold, a mamluk came to me from the house of the Ṣāḥib in Damascus and said: Come and speak with my master.
sentences.n: 'Fī yawmin min al-ayyām' ('on one of the days') is the storyteller's 'one day', and 'idhā' ('behold') marks the sudden arrival. Tānī is printed without the initial alif of atānī ('came to me'); the alif has simply dropped out, and I read the word as the verb it must be. 'Kallim sayyidī' I take as the imperative, 'speak with my master', i.e. come and see him; the next sentence supports it. Al-Ṣāḥib ('the companion') is a title of viziers and great officials, and a mamluk is a slave-soldier.

sentences.t: فَخَرَجْتُ لَهُ وَتَوَجَّهْتُ مَعَهُ إِلَى مَنْزِلِ الصَّاحِبِ فَدَخَلْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-kharajtu lahu wa-tawajjahtu maʿahu ilā manzili al-ṣāḥibi fa-dakhaltu
sentences.l: So I went-out to-him, and I turned-my-face with him to the dwelling of-the-Ṣāḥib, and I entered,
sentences.i: I went out to him and made my way with him to the Ṣāḥib's house, and went in,

sentences.t: فَرَأَيْتُ فِي صَدْرِ الْإِيوَانِ سَرِيرًا مِنَ الْعَرْعَرِ مُصَفَّحًا بِصَفَائِحِ الذَّهَبِ وَعَلَيْهِ آدَمِيٌّ مَرِيضٌ رَاقِدٌ وَهُوَشَابٌّ لَمْ يُرَأَحْسَنُ مِنْهُ فِي الشَّبَابِ
sentences.tr: fa-raʾaytu fī ṣadri al-īwāni sarīran min al-ʿarʿari muṣaffaḥan bi-ṣafāʾiḥi al-dhahabi wa-ʿalayhi ādamiyyun marīḍun rāqidun wa-huwa shābbun lam yura aḥsanu minhu fī al-shabābi
sentences.l: and I saw at the breast of-the-iwan a couch of the juniper, plated with plates of-gold, and upon-it a human, sick, lying; and-he [was] a-youth, there-was-not-seen a-fairer than-him among youth.
sentences.i: and in the upper part of the iwan I saw a couch of juniper wood, plated with sheets of gold, and on it lay a sick man, a youth, the fairest ever seen among the young.
sentences.n: An iwan is a great vaulted hall open on one side, and its ṣadr, its 'breast', is the place of honour at the upper end. Ādamī, 'a son of Adam', is just 'a man'. The print joins wa-huwa shābb into one word, and likewise lam yur + aḥsan into 'lam yurāḥsan'; I read the verb as a passive, 'none fairer was seen'.

sentences.t: فَقَعَدْتُ عِنْدَرَأْسِهِ وَدَعَوْتُ لَهُ بِالشِّفَاءِ فَأَشَارَ إِلَيَّ بِعَيْنِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qaʿadtu ʿinda raʾsihi wa-daʿawtu lahu bi-al-shifāʾi fa-ashāra ilayya bi-ʿaynihi
sentences.l: So I sat at his head, and I prayed for-him with-the-healing, and he signalled to-me with his eye.
sentences.i: I sat down at his head and prayed for his recovery, and he made a sign to me with his eye.
sentences.n: The print joins ʿinda raʾsihi ('at his head') into one word. Daʿā lahu bi- is the verb's own preposition: 'pray for him for (his) healing'. He signs with his eye because he is too weak to speak.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ يَاسَيِّدِي نَاوِلْنِي يَدَ بِسَلَامَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu yā sayyidī nāwilnī yada bi-salāmatika
sentences.l: So I said to-him: O my master, hand-me a-hand, with your safety.
sentences.i: I said to him: My lord, give me your hand, if you please.
sentences.n: Bi-salāmatika ('with your well-being') is a courteous 'if you please'. The print has yad with no suffix; I read it as the bare noun, 'the hand', a physician asking for the pulse, though it may be a slip for yadaka ('your hand'). The print joins yā sayyidī into one word.

sentences.t: فَأَخْرَجَ لِي يَدَةُ الْيُسْرَى فَتَعَجَّبْتُ مِنْ ذَلِكَ وَقُلْتُ لَهُ
sentences.tr: fa-akhraja lī yadahu al-yusrā fa-taʿajjabtu min dhālika wa-qultu lahu
sentences.l: So he brought-out to-me his hand, the left, and I marvelled at that, and I said to-him:
sentences.i: He held out his left hand to me, and I marvelled at that, and I said to him:
sentences.n: The print spells yadahu ('his hand') with a tā marbūṭa (يدة) instead of the pronoun hā'; it is the same -hu, and I read it so. Offering the left hand to a physician is the surprise: the right hand is the one for greeting and giving, as the following words show.

sentences.t: يَا اللَّهُ الْعَجَبُ هَذَا شَابٌّ مَلِيحٌ وَمِنْ بَيْتٍ كَبِيرٍ وَنَاقِصُ أَدَبٍ هَذَا هُوَ الْعَجَبُ
sentences.tr: yā allāhu al-ʿajabu hādhā shābbun malīḥun wa-min baytin kabīrin wa-nāqiṣu adabin hādhā huwa al-ʿajabu
sentences.l: O God, the wonder! This [is] a-youth, handsome, and from a-house great, and lacking-of manners; this, it [is] the wonder.
sentences.i: God above, what a marvel! A handsome young man, of a great house, and yet lacking in manners; that is the marvel.
sentences.n: 'Qultu lahu' is printed ('I said to him'), but what follows reads like the doctor's thought as much as speech, and the story gives no reply. 'Yā allāh' is an exclamation of astonishment, not a prayer. Nāqiṣ adab, 'short of manners', is the doctor's verdict on a patient who offers the wrong hand.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ جَسَيْتُ مَفَاصِلَهُ وَكَتَبْتُ لَهُ وَرَقَةً وَقَعَدْتُ أَتَرَدَّدُ عَلَيْهِ مُدَّةَ عَشَرَةِ أَيَّامٍ حَتَّى تَعَافَى وَدَخَلَ الْحَمَّامَ وَاغْتَسَلَ وَخَرَجَ
sentences.tr: thumma jasaytu mafāṣilahu wa-katabtu lahu waraqatan wa-qaʿadtu ataraddadu ʿalayhi muddata ʿasharati ayyāmin ḥattā taʿāfā wa-dakhala al-ḥammāma wa-ightasala wa-kharaja
sentences.l: Then I felt his joints, and I wrote for-him a sheet, and I sat [i.e. kept] going-to-and-fro to him a period of ten days until he recovered and entered the bath and washed and went-out,
sentences.i: Then I felt his joints and wrote him a prescription, and for ten days I kept going back and forth to attend him, until he recovered, went into the bath, washed, and came out;
sentences.n: Jasaytu is the vernacular form, as if from a final-weak root; Classical has jasastu, from jassa 'to feel (the pulse)'. Waraqa, 'a sheet', is the prescription. 'Qaʿadtu + imperfect' means 'I kept on doing', and taraddada ʿalā is 'to visit repeatedly'.

sentences.t: فَخَلَعَ عَلَيَّ الصَّاحِبُ خِلْعَةً مَلِيحَةً وَجَعَلَنِي مُبَاشِرًا عِنْدَهُ فِى الْمَارِسْتَانِ الَّذِي بِدِ مَشْقَ
sentences.tr: fa-khalaʿa ʿalayya al-ṣāḥibu khilʿatan malīḥatan wa-jaʿalanī mubāshiran ʿindahu fī al-māristāni alladhī bi-Dimashqa
sentences.l: and the Ṣāḥib stripped-upon me a robe-of-honour, handsome, and made me an overseer with him in the hospital which [is] in Damascus.
sentences.i: and the Ṣāḥib bestowed a fine robe of honour on me and appointed me his overseer at the hospital in Damascus.
sentences.n: Khalaʿa ʿalā is the idiom for conferring a robe of honour (khilʿa) on a person, literally 'to strip off upon him'. A māristān (from Persian) is a hospital, and a mubāshir is a supervisor. The print splits 'bi-dimashq' into two pieces, 'bi-d' and 'mashq'; I vocalise the pieces and read them as one word.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا دَخَلْتُ مَعَهُ الْحَمَّامَ وَخَلَّيْتُ لَهُ الْحَمَّامَ جَمِيعَهُ وَدَخَلَتِ الْخَدَمُ بِالشَّابِّ وَأَخَذُوا ثِيَابَهُ مِنْ دَاخِلِ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā dakhaltu maʿahu al-ḥammāma wa-khallaytu lahu al-ḥammāma jamīʿahu wa-dakhalati al-khadamu bi-al-shābbi wa-akhadhū thiyābahu min dākhili al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: And when I entered with him the bath, and I left to-him the bath, all-of-it, and the servants entered with the youth, and took his clothes from the inside of-the-bath,
sentences.i: When I went into the bath with him and had the whole bath cleared for him, the servants came in with the young man and took his clothes inside the bath,
sentences.n: Khallā lahu al-ḥammām is 'to leave the bath to him', that is, to empty it of other bathers. Al-khadam is a collective, so it takes a feminine singular verb (dakhalat).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَعَرَّى رَأَيْتُ يَدَهُ الْيَمِينَ قُطِعَتْ قَرِيبَ الْعَهْدِ وَهُوَ سَبَبُ ضَعْفِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā taʿarrā raʾaytu yadahu al-yamīna quṭiʿat qarība al-ʿahdi wa-huwa sababu ḍaʿfihi
sentences.l: and when he was stripped I saw his hand, the right, cut-off, near of-acquaintance, and it [was] the cause of-his weakness.
sentences.i: and when he was undressed I saw that his right hand had been cut off, and not long before; that was the cause of his weakness.
sentences.n: 'Qarīb al-ʿahd' ('near in acquaintance') means 'recent'. The accusative al-yamīn after yadahu is as printed. This clause finally supplies the main verb that the preceding 'when…' clauses were waiting for.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُهُ أَخَذْتُ أَتَعَجَّبُ وَ حَزِنْتُ عَلَيْهِ وَنَظَرْتُ إِلَى جَسَدِهِ فَوَجَدْتُ عَلَيْهِ آثَارَ ضَرْبِ مَقَارِعَ وَاسْتَعْمَلَ الْأَدْهَانَ لِأَ جْلِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytuhu akhadhtu ataʿajjabu wa-ḥazintu ʿalayhi wa-naẓartu ilā jasadihi fa-wajadtu ʿalayhi āthāra ḍarbi maqāriʿa wa-istaʿmala al-adhāna li-ajli dhālika
sentences.l: So when I saw it I took [to] marvelling, and I grieved over him, and I looked at his body, and I found upon him marks of the striking of whips, and he had used the ointments for the sake of that.
sentences.i: When I saw it, I began to marvel, and I grieved for him. I looked over his body and found on it the marks of a flogging with whips, and signs that he had used salves on account of them.
sentences.n: 'Akhadhtu + imperfect' means 'I began to…'. A miqraʿa (plural maqāriʿ) is a whip or scourge. I read the last verb as active, 'he had used the salves'. The print splits li-ajli into 'li-ʾa' and 'jli' (the two pieces here), a printer's gap inside one word. In the print a lone wāw, 'wa', stands apart from ḥazintu; it is the same 'and'.

sentences.t: فَتَوَسْوَسْتُ لِذَلِكَ وَبَانَ فِي وَجْهِي
sentences.tr: fa-tawaswastu li-dhālika wa-bāna fī wajhī
sentences.l: So I was-uneasy-in-mind because-of that, and it appeared in my face.
sentences.i: I was troubled in my mind at the sight, and it showed in my face.
sentences.n: Tawaswasa is 'to be seized by whisperings of worry', here simply 'to feel uneasy'.

sentences.t: فَنَظَرَ إِلَيَّ الشَّابُّ وَفَهِمَ عَنِّي الْأَمْرَ وَقَالَ لَى يَا حَكِيمَ الزَّمَانِ لَاتَعْجَبْ مِنْ أَمْرِي فَسَوْفَ أُحَدِّثُكَ بِحَدِيثِي حَتَّى تَخْرُجَ مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ
sentences.tr: fa-naẓara ilayya al-shābbu wa-fahima ʿannī al-amra wa-qāla lī yā ḥakīma al-zamāni lā-taʿjab min amrī fa-sawfa uḥaddithuka bi-ḥadīthī ḥattā takhruja mina al-ḥammāmi
sentences.l: The youth looked at me, and understood from me the matter, and said to-me: O sage of-the-age, do-not-marvel at my affair, for soon I-will-tell-you my tale until you go-out of the bath.
sentences.i: The young man looked at me and understood what troubled me, and said: Physician of the age, do not marvel at my case; I shall tell you my story by the time you are out of the bath.
sentences.n: Ḥakīm means both 'sage' and 'physician', so 'ḥakīm al-zamān' flatters the doctor as the wise man of his time. 'Lā-taʿjab' (prohibition) is printed as one word. 'Fahima ʿannī' is 'understood (it) from me', that is, read my face. 'Ḥattā takhruja' ('until you go out') is best rendered 'by the time you are out'.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا خَرَجْنَا مِنَ الْحَمَّامِ وَأَتَيْنَا إِلَى الدَّارِ وَأَكَلْنَا الطَّعَامَ وَاسْتَرَحْنَا فَقَالَ الشَّابُّ هَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تَتَفَرَّجَ فِي الْغُرْفَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kharajnā mina al-ḥammāmi wa-atayna ilā al-dāri wa-akalnā al-ṭaʿāma wa-istaraḥnā fa-qāla al-shābbu hal laka an tatafarraja fī al-ghurfati
sentences.l: And when we went-out from the bath, and came to the house, and ate the food, and rested, the youth said: Is-there to-you that you amuse-yourself in the upper-room?
sentences.i: When we had come out of the bath, returned to the house, eaten, and rested, the young man said: Would you care to take your ease in the upper room?
sentences.n: 'Hal laka an…' ('is there for you that…') is the polite 'would you like to…'. Tafarraja is 'to relax, to take in the view', and al-ghurfa is an upper room, as in the next lines.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ نَعَمْ فَأَمَرَ الْعَبِيدَ أَنْ يُطْلِعُوا الْفُرُشَ إِلَى فَوْقٍ وَأَمَرَهُمْ أَنْ يَشْوُ وْاخَرُوفًا وَأَنْ يَأْتُوا إِلَيْنَا بِفَاكِهَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu naʿam fa-amara al-ʿabīda an yuṭliʿū al-furusha ilā fawqin wa-amarahum an yashwū kharūfan wa-an yaʾtū ilaynā bi-fākihatin
sentences.l: So I said: Yes. And he ordered the slaves to bring-up the furnishings to above, and ordered them to roast a lamb, and to come to-us with fruit.
sentences.i: I said yes, and he ordered the slaves to carry the carpets and cushions up to the top, to roast a lamb, and to bring us fruit.
sentences.n: The print splits the verb 'yashwū kharūfan' wrongly as 'yashw' + 'wākhrūfan': the plural ending wāw and its silent alif have landed on the next word. I vocalise the pieces as printed and read 'yashwū kharūfan', 'that they roast a lamb'. 'Ilā fawq' is 'up above', that is, upstairs. Amara takes its command with 'an', and 'yaʾtū … bi-' is the verb with its own preposition: 'bring (with) …'.

sentences.t: فَأَتَوُا الْعَبِيدُ بِالْفَاكِهَةِ فَأَكَلْنَا وَأَكَلَ هُوَ بِيَدِهِ الشِّمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-atawu al-ʿabīdu bi-al-fākihati fa-akalnā wa-akala huwa bi-yadihi al-shimāli
sentences.l: So they-came, the slaves, with the fruit, and we ate, and he ate with his hand, the left.
sentences.i: The slaves brought the fruit, and we ate; and he ate with his left hand.
sentences.n: Atawu al-ʿabīd, 'they came, the slaves', puts a plural verb before its plural subject, a common vernacular pattern. 'Atā bi-' is 'to bring'. He eats with the left because he has no right hand; the sentence tells you that before he does.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُ حَدِّثْنِي بِحَدِيثِكَ فَقَالَ لِي يَا حَكِيمَ الزَّمَانِ اسْمَعْ مَا جَرَى لِي
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahu ḥaddithnī bi-ḥadīthika fa-qāla lī yā ḥakīma al-zamāni ismaʿ mā jarā lī
sentences.l: So I said to-him: Tell-me your tale. So he said to-me: O sage of-the-age, hear what happened to-me.
sentences.i: I said to him: Tell me your story. He said to me: Physician of the age, hear what befell me.

sentences.t: اِعْلَمْ أَنَّنِي مِنْ أَوْلَادِ الْمَوْصِلِ وَكَانَ لِي وَالِدٌ
sentences.tr: iʿlam annanī min awlādi al-Mawṣili wa-kāna lī wālidun
sentences.l: Know that-I [am] from the children of-Mosul, and there-was to-me a father.
sentences.i: Know that I am a son of Mosul, and I had a father.
sentences.n: 'Awlād al-Mawṣil', 'children of Mosul', means a native of the city.

sentences.t: تُوُفِّيَ وَالِدُهُ وَخَلَّفَ عَشَرَةَ أَوْلَادٍ ذُكُورٍ مِنْ جُمْلَتِهِمْ وَالِدِي يَا حَكِيمُ وَكَانَ أَكْبَرَهُمْ
sentences.tr: tuwuffiya wāliduhu wa-khallafa ʿasharata awlādin dhukūrin min jumlatihim wālidī yā ḥakīmu wa-kāna akbarahum
sentences.l: His father was-taken [i.e. died], and left ten children, males, from the totality of-them my father, O sage, and he was the-eldest-of-them.
sentences.i: His own father died and left ten sons, among them my father, O physician, who was the eldest of them.
sentences.n: The print gives no word for 'my grandfather', so 'his father' (wāliduhu) is the father of my father. 'Yā ḥakīm' is the same address as 'ḥakīm al-zamān', shortened. The stock phrase 'min jumlatihim' means 'among them'.

sentences.t: فَكَبِرَ الْجَمِيعُ وَتَزَوَّجُوا وَرُزِقَ وَالِدِي بِي وَأَمَّا إِخْوَتُهُ التِّسْعَةُ فَلَمْ يُرْزَقُوا بِأَوْلَادٍ
sentences.tr: fa-kabira al-jamīʿu wa-tazawwajū wa-ruziqa wālidī bī wa-ammā ikhwatuhu al-tisʿatu fa-lam yurzaqū bi-awlādin
sentences.l: So grew-up the all, and married, and was-provided my father with-me; and as-for his brothers, the nine, they-were-not provided with children.
sentences.i: They all grew up and married, and my father was blessed with me; but his nine brothers were granted no children.
sentences.n: 'Ruziqa bi-' is the verb's own preposition: 'to be provided with', the usual way of saying a child was granted. The 'wa-ammā … fa-' frame sets the nine brothers against my father.

sentences.t: فَكَبِرْتُ أَنَا وَصِرْتُ بَيْنَ أَعْمَامِي وَهُمْ فَرِحِينَ بِي فَرَحًا شَدِيدًا
sentences.tr: fa-kabirtu anā wa-ṣirtu bayna aʿmāmī wa-hum fariḥīna bī farḥan shadīdan
sentences.l: So I grew-up, I, and I became among my paternal-uncles, and they [being] glad-ones with-me a-joy intense.
sentences.i: I grew up among my uncles, who were overjoyed with me.
sentences.n: 'Wa-hum fariḥīna' puts the plural in the oblique case where Classical would write fariḥūna; the vernacular uses one plural form, and I vocalise it as printed. 'Fariḥa bi-' is 'to rejoice in'. The cognate 'farḥan shadīdan' ('an intense joy') is the intensifier.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَبِرْتُ وَبَلَغْتُ مَبْلَغَ الرِّجَالِ كُنْتُ ذَاتَ يَوْمٍ فِي جَامِعِ الْمَوْصِلِ وَكَانَ يَوْمَ جُمُعَةٍ وَوَالِدِي مَعَنَا وَصَلَّيْنَا الْجُمُعَةَ وَخَرَجَ النَّاسُ جَمِيعًا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kabirtu wa-balaghtu mabligha al-rijāli kuntu dhāta yawmin fī jāmiʿi al-Mawṣili wa-kāna yawma jumuʿatin wa-wālidī maʿanā wa-ṣallaynā al-jumuʿata wa-kharaja al-nāsu jamīʿan
sentences.l: And when I grew-up and reached the reaching-place of-the-men, I was on-a-day in the congregational-mosque of-Mosul; and it-was a-day of-Friday, and my father with-us; and we prayed the Friday, and went-out the people, all.
sentences.i: When I had grown up and come to the full stature of manhood, I was one day in the great mosque of Mosul. It was a Friday and my father was with us; we prayed the Friday prayer, and all the people went out.
sentences.n: 'Dhāta yawmin' ('on a day', literally 'possessor of a day') is the storyteller's 'one day'. Al-jāmiʿ is the congregational mosque, where the Friday prayer is held. 'Wa-kāna yawma jumuʿatin' puts the day in the accusative, as printed.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا وَالِدِي وَأَعْمَامِي فَإِنَّهُمْ قَعَدُوا يَتَحَدَّثُونَ فِي عَجَائِبِ الْبِلَادِ وَغَرَائِبِ الْمُدُنِ إِلَى أَنْ ذَكَرُوا مِصْرَ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā wālidī wa-aʿmāmī fa-innahum qaʿadū yatahaddathūna fī ʿajāʾibi al-bilādi wa-gharāʾibi al-muduni ilā an dhakarū Miṣra
sentences.l: And as-for my father and my paternal-uncles, then-indeed-they sat conversing about the wonders of-the-lands and the marvels of-the-cities, until they mentioned Egypt.
sentences.i: As for my father and my uncles, they stayed on, talking of the wonders of the lands and the marvels of the cities, until they came to mention Egypt.
sentences.n: 'Qaʿadū yatahaddathūn' ('they sat conversing') uses 'sat' in the sense of 'went on'. The two hamzas of ʿajāʾib and gharāʾib are printed in the edition itself.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ أَعْمَامِي يَقُولُ الْمُسَافِرُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla aʿmāmī yaqūlu al-musāfirūna
sentences.l: So said my paternal-uncles: Say the travellers,
sentences.i: My uncles said: The travellers say,
sentences.n: This is a fragment; the uncles' report about Egypt continues in the next unit.

sentences.t: إِنَّمَا عَلَى وَجْهِ الْأَرْضِ أَحْسَنُ مِنْ مِصْرَ وَنِيلِهَا
sentences.tr: innamā ʿalā wajhi al-arḍi aḥsanu min Miṣra wa-nīlihā
sentences.l: Indeed-not [is there] on the face of the earth [anything] finer than Miṣr and its Nile
sentences.i: There is nothing on the face of the earth finer than Egypt and its Nile.
sentences.n: The travellers' words begin here, after the quoting verb that ends the previous unit. The print runs inna and mā together; I read them as 'inna mā' with mā in a negative sense, since the claim is plainly that Egypt has no equal. If instead it is innamā, 'only', the sentence is rougher but the praise is the same. Miṣr is Egypt as a land (and, as often in the Nights, its capital, Cairo).

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعْتُ هَذَا الْكَلَامَ تَشَوَّقْتُ إِلَى مِصْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿtu hādhā al-kalāma tashawwaqtu ilā Miṣra
sentences.l: So when I heard this the-speech, I longed to Miṣr,
sentences.i: And when I heard this talk, I was seized with longing for Egypt.
sentences.n: The narrator is the young man of the tale, speaking in the first person; his father's praise of Egypt is what first sets him longing. tashawwaqa ilā, 'to long toward', takes ilā, as the print has it.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ وَالِدِي مَنْ لَارَى الْمِصْرَ مَا رَأَى الدُّنْيَا تُرَابُهَا ذَهَبٌ وَنِيلُهَا عَجَبٌ وَنِسَاؤُهَا حُورٌ وَبُيُوتُهَا قُصُورٌ وَهَوَا ؤُهَا مُعْتَدِلٌ يَفُوقُ عَرْفُهُ الْكِبَا وَيُخْجِلُ
sentences.tr: thumma qāla wālidī man lārā al-Miṣra mā raʾā al-dunyā turābuhā dhahabun wa-nīluhā ʿajabun wa-nisāʾuhā ḥūrun wa-buyūtuhā quṣūrun wa-hawāʾuhā muʿtadilun yafūqu ʿarfuhu al-kibā wa-yukhjilu
sentences.l: Then my-father said: Whoever not-saw al-Miṣr has not seen the world; its dust [is] gold, and its Nile [is] a wonder, and its women [are] houris, and its houses [are] palaces, and its air [is] temperate; its fragrance surpasses the aloes-wood and shames.
sentences.i: Then my father said: 'Whoever has not seen Egypt has not seen the world. Its dust is gold, its Nile a wonder, its women houris, its houses palaces, its air temperate; its fragrance surpasses aloes-wood and puts it to shame.'
sentences.n: Note the rhyming, balanced clauses (sajʿ): turābuhā dhahab, nīluhā ʿajab, nisāʾuhā ḥūr, buyūtuhā quṣūr. The print has lārā, which looks like lā yarā or lam yara with the yāʾ dropped: 'who has not seen'. I vocalise what is printed (lā plus a perfect rā for raʾā), and the sense is clear. The edition also splits hawā ʾuhā into two pieces, and prints al-kibā without its final hamza; I follow both. The verb yukhjilu has no object in the print (the aloes-wood is the natural one, or perhaps ambergris or musk has dropped out).

sentences.t: وَكَيْفَ لَا تَكُونُ كَذَلِكَ وَهِيَ الدُّنْيَا وَلِلَّهِ دَرُّ مَنْ قَالَ شِ—رٌ
sentences.tr: wa-kayfa lā takūnu kadhālika wa-hiya al-dunyā wa-li-allāhi darru man qāla shiʿrun
sentences.l: And how not would-it-be so, and she [is] the world? And to God [is] the milk-flow of him who said verse:
sentences.i: And how could it be otherwise, when it is the whole world? Well said the man who said, in verse:
sentences.n: 'For God is the dar of whoever said …' (li-llāhi darru man qāla) is a stock phrase of admiration: lit. 'to God belongs the milk-flow of the one who said', i.e. what a gift he has! The last word is printed shiʿr with a dash in place of the ʿayn, a printer's abbreviation for shiʿr, 'verse'; I read it shiʿrun.

sentences.t:
اَاَرْحَلُ عَنْ مِصْرٍ وَطِيبِ نَعِيمِهَا * وَاَيُّ مَكَانٍ بَعْدَ هَالِيَ شَائِقُ
وَاَتْرُكُ اَوْطَانًا تَرَاهَا لِنَا شِقِ * هُوَالطِّيبُ لَامَا ضَمَّنَتْهُ الْمَفَارِقُ
وَكَيْفَ وَقَدْ اَضْحَتْ مِنَ الْحُسْنِ جَنَّةً * زَرَابِيُّهَا مَبْثُوثَةٌ وَالنَّمَارِقُ
بِلَادٌ تَشُوقُ الْعَيْنَ وَالْقَلْبَ بَهْجَةً * وَتَجْمَعُ مَا يَهْوَى تَقِيٌّ وَفَاسِقُ
وَاِخْوَانُ صِدْقٍ يَجْمَعُ الْفَضْلُ شَمْلَهُمْ * مَجَالِسُهُمْ مِمَّا حَوَوْهُ حَدَائِقُ
اَسُكَّانَ مِصْرَانْ قَضَى اللهُ بِالنَّوَى * فَتَمَّ عُهُودٌ بَيْنَنَا وَمَوَاثِقُ
فَلَا تَذْكُرُوهَا لِلنَّسِيمِ فَاِنَّهُ * لِاَمْثَالِهَا مِنْ نَفْحَةِ الرَّوْضِ سَارِقُ
sentences.tr:
a-arḥalu ʿan Miṣrin wa-ṭībi naʿīmihā * wa-ayyu makānin baʿda hāliya shāʾiqu
wa-atruku awṭānan tarāhā li-nāshiqi * huwa al-ṭību lā mā ḍammanat-hu al-mafāriqu
wa-kayfa wa-qad aḍḥat mina al-ḥusni jannatan * zarābiyyuhā mabthūthatun wa-al-namāriqu
bilādun tashūqu al-ʿayna wa-al-qalba bahjatan * wa-tajmaʿu mā yahwā taqiyyun wa-fāsiqu
wa-ikhwānu ṣidqin yajmaʿu al-faḍlu shamlahum * majālisuhum mimmā ḥawawhu ḥadāʾiqu
a-sukkāna Miṣra in qaḍā allāhu bi-al-nawā * fa-tamma ʿuhūdun baynanā wa-mawāthiqu
fa-lā tadhkurūhā li-al-nasīmi fa-innahu * li-amthālihā min nafḥati al-rawḍi sāriqu
sentences.l:
Shall-I depart from Miṣr and the goodness of its bliss? * And what place after hāliya [obscure] would be alluring?
And shall-I leave homelands you-see-them for a-sniffer? * It is the perfume, not what the hair-partings hold!
And how, when it has become, from beauty, a garden * its carpets scattered-abroad, and the cushions?
Lands that-allure the eye and the heart with splendour * and gather what the pious and the sinner love,
And brothers of truth whose company Virtue gathers * their assemblies, from what they enclose, are gardens.
O dwellers-of Miṣr, if God has decreed with the parting * then are-complete covenants between us, and pledges.
So do-not mention-it to the breeze, for it * of the like of it, from the waft of the meadow, is a thief.
sentences.i:
Shall I depart from Egypt and the sweetness of its ease? And what place, after this, could ever allure me?
Shall I forsake homelands that seem to the one who breathes them in the very perfume itself, and not merely what the hair-partings hold?
And how, when from sheer beauty it has become a garden, its carpets spread abroad and its cushions laid out?
Lands that delight the eye and the heart with splendour, and gather what both the pious man and the sinner desire,
And brothers of truth, whom virtue binds in fellowship, whose gatherings, by what they hold, are gardens.
O dwellers of Egypt, if God has decreed our parting, then the covenants and pledges between us stand fulfilled.
So do not speak of her to the breeze, for it steals the likes of her from the fragrance of the meadow.
sentences.n: Seven lines of verse in the tawīl metre, copied exactly as the edition prints and points them. The verse is a farewell to Egypt, set in the father's mouth. Line 1: hāliya is obscure as printed; it may be hā lī, 'this, for me', or a slip for ḥālī, 'my state', and I would not lean on it. Line 2: li-nāshiqin is printed li-nā shiqi (two pieces); nāshiq is 'one who inhales'. The perfume-in-the-partings image is of scent applied to the parting of the hair. Line 3 borrows the Qurʾan's carpets (zarābiyyu mabthūtha) and cushions (namāriq) of Paradise (Q 88:15-16). Line 6: the print has Miṣrān, which I read as Miṣra in (a run-together 'if'), with the sukūn on the nūn as printed; mawāthiq is plural of mīthāq.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ قَالَ وَالِدِي وَلَوْ رَأَيْتُمْ رِيَاضَهَا بِالْأَ صَائِلِ وَالظِّلُّ عَلَيْهَا مَائِلٌ لَشَاهَدْتُمْ عَجَبًا وَمِلْتُمْ لَهَا طَرَبًا
sentences.tr: thumma qāla wālidī wa-law raʾaytum riyāḍahā bi-al-aṣāʾili wa-al-ẓillu ʿalayhā māʾilun la-shāhadtum ʿajaban wa-miltum lahā ṭaraban
sentences.l: Then my-father said: And if you-had-seen its gardens in the late-afternoons, and the shade upon them leaning, you-would-have-beheld a wonder, and you-would-have-inclined to them in delight.
sentences.i: Then my father said: 'And had you seen its gardens in the late afternoons, with the shade leaning across them, you would have beheld a wonder and bent toward them in delight.'
sentences.n: The print splits bi-al-aṣāʾil into two pieces (bi-al-ʾa and ṣāʾil), as it does with a few other words in this passage; I keep the printed division. Notice the hint of a rhyme in māʾil and the verb la-shāhadtum; 'inclined' (miltum) plays on the leaning shade.

sentences.t: قَالَ وَأَخَذُوا يُوَصِّفُونَ مِصْرَ وَنِيلَهَا
sentences.tr: qāla wa-akhadhū yuwaṣṣifūna Miṣra wa-nīlahā
sentences.l: He said: and they took to-describing Miṣr and its Nile.
sentences.i: He said: and they all fell to describing Egypt and its Nile.
sentences.n: The young man speaks again after his father's quotation. akhadha plus a present verb, 'to begin to do', is common in the Nights. yuwaṣṣifūna is the intensive (form II) of 'describe', here with the sense of 'describe at length'.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغُوا وَسَمِعْتُ أَنَا هَذِهِ الْأَوْصَافَ الَّتِي فِي مِصْرَ بَقِيَ خَاطِرِي فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghū wa-samiʿtu anā hādhihi al-awṣāfa allatī fī Miṣra baqiya khāṭirī fīhā
sentences.l: So when they finished, and I heard, I, these the-descriptions which [are] in Miṣr, my mind remained in it.
sentences.i: When they had finished, and I had heard all these descriptions of Egypt, my mind remained fixed upon it.
sentences.n: A long when-clause whose main verb, baqiya khāṭirī, only arrives at the end: 'my mind stayed on her'. The pronoun anā ('I') is the print's, and stresses the narrator.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَرَغُوا وَقَامَ كُلُّ وَاحِدٍ تَوَجَّهَ إِلَى مَنْزِلِهِ نِمْتُ تِلْكَ اللَّيْلَةَ لَمْ يَأْتِنِي نَوْمٌ مِنْ شَغَفِي بِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā faraghū wa-qāma kullu wāḥidin tawajjaha ilā manzilihi nimtu tilka al-laylata lam yaʾtinī nawmun min shaghafī bihā
sentences.l: So when they finished and each one arose, he went-toward his house, I lay-down that night, not came-to-me sleep from my passion for-her.
sentences.i: When they had finished, and each man had risen and gone to his house, I lay down that night, but no sleep came to me, from my passion for her.
sentences.n: 'Each one arose, he went': two verbs side by side with no 'and', which the Arabic allows. The 'her' is Egypt, treated as a feminine beloved.

sentences.t: وَ مَا بَقِيَ يَهْنَئُ لِي أَكْلٌ وَلَا شُرْبٌ
sentences.tr: wa-mā baqiya yahnaʾu lī aklun wa-lā shurbun
sentences.l: And no-longer was-wholesome to-me eating nor drinking.
sentences.i: Nor was food or drink any longer pleasant to me.
sentences.n: The print puts a space after the wa- and prints the verb as yahniʾ with the hamza on a yāʾ-seat and no case vowel; I read it as yahnaʾu, 'is wholesome'. mā baqiya, 'no longer', is a Middle Arabic idiom for 'no more'.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَ بَعْدَ أَيَّامٍ قَلَائِلَ تَجَهَّزَ أَعْمَامِي إِلَى مِصْرَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kāna baʿda ayyāmin qalāʾila tajahhaza aʿmāmī ilā Miṣra
sentences.l: So when it was after days few, my-paternal-uncles equipped-themselves to Miṣr.
sentences.i: And when, after a few days, my uncles made ready for the journey to Egypt,
sentences.n: tajahhaza ilā is 'to prepare for a journey to'. The uncles are his father's brothers, merchants. The sentence runs into the next, where the main clause lies.

sentences.t: فَبَكَيْتُ عَلَى وَالِدِي حَتَّى جَهَّزَلِي مَتْجَرًا وَمَضَيْتُ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-bakaytu ʿalā wālidī ḥattā jahhazalī matjaran wa-maḍaytu maʿahum
sentences.l: I wept upon my-father until he-equipped-for-me merchandise, and I went with them.
sentences.i: I wept before my father until he fitted me out with a stock of merchandise, and I went off with them.
sentences.n: The print joins jahhaza and lī into one word, jahhazalī. matjar means a merchant's stock, or a trading venture.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُمْ لَا تَدَعُوهُ يَدْخُلُ مِصْرَ وَدَعُوهُ يَبِيعُ مَتْجَرَهُ بِدِمَشْقَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahum lā tadaʿūhu yadkhulu Miṣra wa-daʿūhu yabīʿu matjarahu bi-Dimashqa
sentences.l: And he said to-them: Do-not leave him enter Miṣr, and leave him sell his-merchandise in Damascus.
sentences.i: And he said to them: 'Do not let him enter Egypt; let him sell his goods in Damascus.'
sentences.n: The father is speaking to his brothers. 'Leave him do' (daʿūhu yabīʿu) is the colloquial way of saying 'let him do', with the second verb simply in the present and no linking particle. The father fears for the boy's safety in Egypt, as the story soon shows.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَافَرْنَا وَوَدَّعْتُ وَالِدِي وَخَرَجْنَا مِنَ الْمَوْصِلِ وَمَا زِلْنَا مُسَافِرِينَ حَتَّى وَصَلْنَا حَلَبَ
sentences.tr: thumma sāfarnā wa-waddaʿtu wālidī wa-kharajnā mina al-Mawṣili wa-mā zilnā musāfirīna ḥattā waṣalnā Ḥalaba
sentences.l: Then we travelled, and I bade-farewell to my-father, and we went-out from al-Mawṣil, and we-did-not cease [being] travellers until we arrived [at] Aleppo.
sentences.i: Then we set out; I bade my father farewell, and we left Mosul and went on traveling until we reached Aleppo.
sentences.n: The tale is set at Mosul. Strictly the farewell comes before the setting out; the print puts them in this order. mā zilnā musāfirīna, 'we did not cease being travellers', is the standard way to say 'we kept on travelling'.

sentences.t: فَأَقَمْنَا بِهَا أَيَّامًا
sentences.tr: fa-aqamnā bihā ayyāman
sentences.l: So we stayed in-it days.
sentences.i: We stayed there some days,

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَافَرْنَا إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلْنَا دِمَشْقَ
sentences.tr: thumma sāfarnā ilā an waṣalnā Dimashqa
sentences.l: Then we travelled until [it was that] we arrived [at] Damascus.
